synthesis.headline: The three-week block finally reconfigures: a cold cutoff drops into the northern Rockies while the Southwest heat dome digs in for the long haul
synthesis.narrative:
The high-amplitude summer block Tlaloc has tracked for roughly three weeks is not resetting, but it is visibly reorganizing — and today marks the turn yesterday's analysis anticipated. Yesterday the block was defined by a fully cut-off low over the Mid-Atlantic and a heat ridge parked over the Rockies. Today those pieces have moved: at 500 mb the eastern cutoff has slid offshore, now just a negatively tilted shortwave and PV streamer curling over southern New England, while a deep, unusually cold cutoff low has dropped onto the Montana-Wyoming border (core heights near 5720 dm). The ridge that governed the West has retreated and elongated from the Gulf of Alaska into central Canada, leaving a classic Rex-block couplet — cold vortex to the south, ridge to the north — that keeps western flow stalled. The practical result is a two-story continent: a hot, largely quiet interior West under the surviving ridge, and an active northern and eastern rim where the new energy is working.

Today's centers of action ring that rim. The busiest is the central Plains, where SPC carries a Slight Risk across Nebraska and South Dakota: a shortwave ejecting from the Wyoming cutoff meets a moisture-rich airmass and a southeastward-sagging cold front, with early supercells (large hail) expected to congeal into a damaging-wind cluster this evening as the low-level jet ramps up. Downstream, WPC flags a Slight Risk of excessive rainfall over the Mid to Lower Missouri and Mississippi Valleys, where training storms along the same front raise the flash-flood threat. To the southeast, deep convection is already firing from Louisiana through Georgia and into Florida along the stalled front and the moist-dry airmass boundary, anchored by a weak 1008 mb Gulf Coast low, while the departing Northeast low keeps a lingering flash-flood risk over New England through Thursday. Beneath the ridge, dangerous heat dominates the South and is set to expand into the Southwest, Intermountain West, and northern High Plains, with heat indices of 105-115 and Major-to-Extreme HeatRisk. Canada carries equal weight today: a deep 979 mb low over Hudson Bay drives gusty northwest flow across Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic Canada against a 1037 mb Atlantic high, while a 1028 mb ridge keeps British Columbia and Alberta settled and a secondary low over the northern Prairies focuses convection along the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border — the northern extension of the same frontal system trailing into the U.S. Plains.

Aloft the structure ties it together. The equatorward flank of the northern-Rockies cutoff hosts a jet streak exceeding 105 knots oriented southwest-to-northeast across the northern Plains, and its negative tilt maximizes dynamic lift over the Upper Midwest — precisely where the severe and heavy-rain threats are concentrated. Air Mass RGB shows the reason in color: a broad orange-red stratospheric dry intrusion sweeps from the northern Rockies through the High Plains into Texas on the trough's back side, with the sharpest boundary against vivid tropical green — the implied jet axis — running from the Upper Midwest southwestward through Kansas and Oklahoma. A second, tighter PV filament over the Northeast marks the closing-off eastern low. Looking ahead, WPC's extended discussion confirms the block breaks down only at its northern edge: a closed low and trailing cold front work inland across southwestern Canada this weekend into Monday, cooling the Pacific Northwest and northern Plains, while the Southwest ridge holds longest and hottest with widespread 110s and record warm overnight lows persisting into next week.
synthesis.climate_context: This is textbook late-July North America. The North American Monsoon is in full swing over the Desert Southwest and southern Rockies, feeding the Four Corners flash-flood and localized severe threats, while peak heat-and-severe season drives both the entrenched interior-West heat dome and the marginal severe threats along the trough's periphery; the CPC 6-10 day outlook keeps a 90-100 percent above-normal bullseye over the Great Basin and interior Southwest, confirming the western ridge only erodes at its northern edge rather than collapsing through early August. The hurricane basins remain split against the climatological ramp toward peak season: the Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf are quiet with no development expected over the next seven days, while the East Pacific stays active with Hurricane Genevieve spinning several hundred miles west of southern Baja California and scattered ITCZ convection near the Panama-Colombia border. The ENSO backdrop is one of steady cold-to-warm transition — after a weak La Nina near -0.5C, the ONI has warmed through neutral into warm-phase territory this year, a shift toward El Nino that tends to enhance shear over the tropical Atlantic and is consistent with the basin's current quiescence, even as it will increasingly shape steering through the back half of the season.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC is monitoring no organized convective threat and has issued no mesoscale discussions in the past six hours. The sharpest sub-synoptic signals are the central Plains severe corridor — supercells over south-central South Dakota into central Nebraska this afternoon transitioning to a damaging-wind cluster this evening as the low-level jet strengthens — and the training heavy rain over the Mid to Lower Missouri and Mississippi Valleys. Elsewhere, watch the lingering New England flash-flood risk behind the exiting Northeast low, North American Monsoon burn-scar and steep-terrain concerns across eastern Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, and dangerous heat (indices 105-115, Major-to-Extreme HeatRisk) across the South and interior West. In Canada, the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border bears watching for organized convection along the secondary Prairie low, while the deep Hudson Bay low keeps gusty northwesterly winds over Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic Canada.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: Valid 1200Z Thursday 30 July 2026. A broad 1020 mb high dominates the central Plains and upper Midwest, with a separate 1017 mb high over the northern Rockies and another centered near 1012 mb over the Canadian Maritimes, collectively suppressing convection across a wide swath of the interior. A sprawling thermal low near 1004 mb sits over the Desert Southwest into northern Mexico, and a secondary low around 1008 mb is positioned over the central Gulf Coast region, with a weak 997 mb low visible near the upper Great Lakes. A stationary or slow-moving front extends from the mid-Atlantic southwestward across the Tennessee Valley and into Texas, and a separate cold front pushes through the Pacific Northwest toward the northern Rockies. Pressure gradients are tightest along the Pacific coast of British Columbia and in the Gulf Coast convergence zone near the 1008 mb low, where moisture pooling and surface confluence are focusing lift for convective development. The axis of deepest moisture and greatest instability appears concentrated across the Gulf States and lower Mississippi Valley, where dewpoints in the mid-70s converge beneath the frontal boundary, supporting the highest thunderstorm threat on this analysis.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
CMC Surface Analysis 0000Z Thursday 30 July 2026

A deep low centered near Hudson Bay at approximately 979 mb is the dominant feature over Canada, with tightly packed isobars on its western and southern flanks indicating a strong pressure gradient across Ontario and Quebec, where surface winds are likely gusty and backed from the northwest behind a well-defined cold front trailing southwestward into the central United States. A strong anticyclone at 1037 mb sits over the central North Atlantic east of Newfoundland, and the pressure contrast between that high and the Hudson Bay low is driving a vigorous northwesterly flow across Atlantic Canada. Over western Canada, a ridge axis with a 1028 mb high over British Columbia and Alberta is maintaining dry, settled conditions, though a weak frontal boundary along the BC-Alberta corridor separates this ridge from the low pressure field to the east. A secondary low complex is evident across the northern Prairie provinces and extending into the Dakotas, with associated frontal boundaries suggesting organized lift and potential convective activity along the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border region. The southern Prairies and upper Midwest share a zone of cyclonic curvature between these systems that could focus moisture return and thunderstorm development northward into southern Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb, the dominant feature is a deep, high-amplitude cutoff low centered over the Montana-Wyoming border region, with the core heights dropping to near 5720 dm and a pronounced cold anomaly of around -40 to -50 degrees C at the center, indicating a very cold, isolated vortex well detached from the main westerly flow. The longwave pattern shows a strongly amplified Rex block configuration, with the cutoff low to the south of a broad ridge axis extending from the Gulf of Alaska into central Canada, effectively stalling progressive flow across the western half of the continent. A strong jet streak is evident on the equatorward side of the cutoff, oriented southwest to northeast across the northern Plains, with winds exceeding 105 knots near the base of the trough, and the trough axis shows a negative tilt, favoring dynamic lift downstream over the Upper Midwest. Along the East Coast, a separate shortwave is digging southward through New England, indicated by the tightening height gradient and the red wind barb marker near coastal New England, with a weakly negative tilt. The overall pattern is decidedly blocked, with the cutoff low likely to be slow-moving and persistent given the upstream ridge anchoring it in place.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 30 July 2026 at 1401Z shows a prominent stratospheric dry intrusion displayed as a deep orange-red swath extending from the northern Rockies and northern Plains southward through the central and southern High Plains into Texas, indicating high potential vorticity air descending from the stratosphere and a well-defined upper-level trough over that region. The implied jet axis runs along the eastern boundary of this orange-red airmass, roughly from the upper Midwest southwestward through Kansas and Oklahoma, where the sharpest contrast with the moist green airmass to the east occurs. A second, tighter PV streamer or possible cutoff signature is visible over the Northeast, centered near southern New England and the Mid-Atlantic, shown by the curling orange-red filament with bright white cloud wrapping around its southern edge, consistent with a closed or nearly closed upper low. Deep convection is evident as bright white cells scattered across the Gulf Coast states from Louisiana through Georgia and peninsular Florida, embedded along the moist-dry airmass boundary where the jet dynamics are promoting lift. The broad green signature dominating the Southeast and Gulf of Mexico confirms a deep layer of tropical moisture in place east of the trough axis.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: At 1400Z on 30 July 2026, a well-defined polar jet streak is evident across the northern tier of Canada and into the North Atlantic, marked by a sharp orange-to-green airmass boundary indicative of high potential vorticity air intruding from high latitudes. A broad stratospheric dry intrusion, rendered in deep orange-red, sweeps from the Canadian Prairies southeastward toward the Great Lakes region, suggesting a significant upper-level trough axis in that vicinity. In the tropics, a bright white deep convective cluster sits near the Panama-Colombia border region, with additional isolated convective cells scattered across the eastern Pacific between roughly 5N and 15N, consistent with disturbances along the ITCZ. The Caribbean basin appears relatively quiescent at this time with no clearly organized tropical wave or closed circulation visible, though modest mid-level moisture in green tones extends from the Lesser Antilles westward through the Gulf. In the Southern Hemisphere, an active mid-latitude cyclone is visible south of Argentina near the Drake Passage, with a classic comma-cloud structure and trailing cold frontal band extending northeastward toward southern Brazil.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a high-probability above-normal signal centered over the Great Basin and interior Southwest, where the darkest shading indicates 90-100% odds of above-normal temperatures across Nevada, Utah, and western Colorado, implying a very robust and persistent upper-level ridge anchored over that region through August 4-8. A secondary above-normal lobe with 70-80% probabilities covers the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast corridor from Pennsylvania through Maine, suggesting either a ridge extension or a separate downstream ridging feature along the East Coast. The only area resisting the warm pattern is a near-normal zone across northern Montana, the Dakotas, and southern Manitoba, which typically reflects a trough axis or at least a neutral upper flow regime over the northern Plains acting as a boundary between the western ridge and any cooler Pacific influence. A small near-normal pocket in central Florida and the eastern Gulf Coast stands out as a localized exception, likely reflecting persistent cloud cover and precipitation associated with a summer convective regime suppressing daytime temperature anomalies. Taken together, the strong, coherent probability gradients from the core of the western ridge outward indicate this is not a transitional pattern but rather a well-established warm regime expected to hold through the valid period with little sign of a significant trough ejection breaking it down.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Flash flooding risk in New England through Thursday from a Northeast low exiting offshore with lingering moisture. Four Corners and Southeast continue Monday through Friday from monsoonal moisture and stationary frontal pooling respectively. Severe thunderstorms and flash flooding likely across Plains and Midwest through Friday as shortwave troughs push a cold front southeastward, creating organized convection with training potential. Slight Risk excessive rainfall over Mid to Lower Missouri/Mississippi Valley; slight severe risk central and northern Plains shifting eastward Friday. Dangerous heat dominates South through Saturday, expanding into Southwest, Intermountain West, and northern High Plains late week into weekend, with heat indices reaching 105-115 degrees and Major to Extreme HeatRisk levels.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: SLIGHT RISK issued for severe thunderstorms across central Plains, primarily Nebraska and South Dakota. Shortwave trough moving east from Wyoming will interact with moisture-rich air mass and southeastward-moving cold front. Early cloud cover will clear, allowing surface heating along trough. Supercells possible south-central South Dakota into central Nebraska early, with severe hail initially; damaging winds expected to dominate as storms cluster and organize upscale this evening, aided by strengthening low-level jet. Isolated to scattered storms possible in High Plains (eastern Colorado, western Kansas, northeast Montana) with localized severe wind and hail. Isolated damaging wind gusts possible across Southeast near frontal boundary where scattered thunderstorms developing.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No organized convective threat is currently being monitored by SPC. No mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the North Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf of America.

East Pacific: Hurricane Genevieve is active several hundred miles west of southern Baja California. No additional tropical cyclone formation expected in the eastern and central North Pacific over the next 7 days.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows weak La Niña conditions currently (SON 2025), with anomalies around -0.5°C. The phase is transitioning toward neutral by early 2026 (JFM), with anomalies approaching zero. By spring 2026, the index strengthens into El Niño territory, with anomalies climbing to +0.98°C by April-June. The overall trend indicates a shift from La Niña through neutral conditions into moderate El Niño development over the next nine months.
